name: Mary Celeste
description: An American brigantine found drifting in good order but completely abandoned in the Atlantic east of the Azores on 4 December 1872; her ten-person company — Captain Benjamin Briggs, his wife and infant daughter, and seven crew — were never seen again.
full_description: The Mary Celeste was a 282-ton American merchant brigantine discovered drifting between the Azores and Portugal on 4 December 1872 by the Canadian brigantine Dei Gratia under Captain David Morehouse. The ship was largely seaworthy under partial sail with cargo (1,701 barrels of denatured alcohol bound for Genoa) intact, but her single lifeboat was missing and her crew gone. The last log entry was dated 25 November 1872. The case was investigated at salvage hearings in Gibraltar from 17 December 1872 by Attorney General Frederick Solly-Flood, whose suspicions of foul play were never substantiated. Subsequent theories include a panicked abandonment due to fears of an alcohol-vapour explosion, a misread sounding of the pumps suggesting the ship was sinking, a waterspout, and seaquake-induced cargo shift. The vessel — built in 1861 at Spencer's Island, Nova Scotia, originally as the Amazon — was deliberately wrecked in 1885 off Haiti by Captain Gilman C. Parker as part of an insurance fraud. Arthur Conan Doyle's fictional 1884 short story 'J. Habakuk Jephson's Statement' is largely responsible for the modern legend, including the spelling 'Marie Celeste'.

aliases.name: Marie Celeste

aliases.name: Amazon
aliases.meaning: Original name of the brigantine before her 1868 sale and renaming

origin: The events occurred in the central North Atlantic, with the abandonment somewhere east of the Azores. The ship was found at approximately 38°20′N 17°15′W, midway between the Azores and the Portuguese coast.

etymology.origin: The brigantine was launched in 1861 at Spencer's Island, Nova Scotia, as the Amazon. After grounding, salvage and resale to American owners in 1868 she was re-registered under the name Mary Celeste.
etymology.meaning: The name combines the English Christian name Mary with celeste, from Latin caelestis ('heavenly').

cultural_notes: The Mary Celeste's modern cultural status as the archetypal 'ghost ship' is largely a 20th-century construction; the historical record itself supports an unromantic, mundane reading.
